source.title: To Align or Not to Align: Strategic Multimodal Representation Alignment for Optimal Performance
source.authors: Wanlong Fang; Tianle Zhang; Alvin Chan

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present, including appendices, though some referenced figures are not rendered with readable plotted values.
record.tranche_reason: The study discusses natural multimodal alignment and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but its experiments deliberately impose alignment with a contrastive loss. They do not test whether naturally arising alignment increases with scale or capability, or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study varies an explicit alignment-loss weight during training and reports alignment and task-performance outcomes. These are results about forced alignment, not evidence of naturally emerging convergence. The text also mentions additional modality-pair plots in Figures 6–7 without describing their outcomes; no specific result is extractable from those plots here.
record.test_reason: The study imposes cross-modal alignment on purpose, using a λ-weighted contrastive loss, and measures task accuracy and alignment as λ varies. It does not measure alignment arising without that objective across scale, capability, seeds or models. The λ=0 baseline is reported only as a starting point, with no comparison bearing on any version. Rising CKA, SVCCA and Mutual-KNN with λ simply show that the loss works. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. One addition: the authors also say their redundancy-dominant results 'empirically support' the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. That is an interpretive claim about forced alignment's benefit, not a test of natural convergence.
record.recipe_differences: The study imposes cross-modal alignment during training using a tunable contrastive loss and measures task accuracy plus CKA, SVCCA, and Mutual-KNN. It does not use the original studies' observational natural-alignment or scaling approach.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with the alignment-loss weight λ and the dataset's redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy structure. Alignment metrics rise with λ across the described cases, while accuracy may improve, decline, or peak and then fall. The text does not report metric-setting sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: Under an imposed contrastive alignment loss, alignment metrics rise monotonically with λ in all reported settings. Unimodal accuracy, however, rises in redundancy-dominant settings, falls in uniqueness-dominant ones, and peaks at an intermediate λ in mixed ones. Examples: MUStARD vision encoder accuracy goes from 0.54 to 0.62; the synthetic R=4 setting peaks at λ≈0.4–0.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Greater enforced cross-modal alignment improves unimodal performance only to the extent that modalities share redundant task-relevant information. Higher alignment scores do not imply better task performance.

record.problems: The reported text gives mostly qualitative trends rather than numerical metric values or uncertainty estimates. The experiment studies forced alignment, not natural alignment across scale or capability. The study describes only selected real-world modality pairs in the main results; additional pairs are referenced in figures without text descriptions here. The paper gives differing statements about repetitions (4 seeds in one section and averages across 5 seeds in another).
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for described main-text results. Additional modality-pair experiments are referenced in Appendix Section 5, Figures 6–7, but their plotted outcomes are not rendered or described in the supplied text, so no results can be assigned.

untested.parts: No scaling or capability sweep and no comparison of independently trained models across architectures, objectives or data.
Vision–text pairs are trained with an imposed contrastive alignment. Natural image–caption alignment as models improve is not measured.
No comparison of same-architecture networks trained from different seeds.
No linear mapping, stitching, relative representations or unpaired translation.
No analysis of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Three metrics are reported together as moving in the same direction under forced alignment. Metric settings, neighbour counts and out-of-distribution inputs are not varied.
No test of whether natural convergence is complete, plateaus, or is caused by shared data or objectives.

record.verdict_notes: The appendix figures (Figures 6–7) for further modality pairs are not described in the text, but they also concern forced alignment and would bear on no version. Repetition counts are inconsistent: 4 seeds in Section 4.1, 5 seeds in Section 4.4, and 3 seeds for synthetic data generation.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability scaling sweep, nor comparison of independently trained models across architectures, objectives, or datasets.
Although vision-text pairs are included, alignment is explicitly induced; the study does not test whether paired vision and language representations align more as both models improve.
No comparison across random initializations of same-architecture networks for shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.

The study uses CKA, SVCCA, and Mutual-KNN, but does not test whether convergence findings change with metric settings or out-of-distribution inputs. It tests how the performance effect of imposed alignment varies with dataset information structure.
No test of natural convergence completeness or plateau, or of whether shared data/objectives rather than a common model of reality explain natural alignment.
